summary: Documents commonly used BGP mechanisms for Autonomous System number migration that are not formally part of BGP-4, and their effect on the AS_PATH attribute, so future BGP work supports them properly.

eli5.summary: When a network changes its ID number, it uses some tricks. This writes those tricks down.

subtitle: The router tricks ISPs use to switch to a new AS number without making every customer reconfigure at once.

tldr.problem: When an ISP merges networks and retires an AS number, its eBGP peers expect the old number, and a longer AS_PATH would shift traffic in other networks.
tldr.mechanism: Local per-neighbor settings let a router open sessions with the old ASN and edit the AS_PATH it stores and sends (Local AS, No Prepend Inbound, Replace Old AS). A separate iBGP setting accepts either ASN inside the network.
tldr.outcome: Customers can migrate when convenient and the AS_PATH length stays the same. The RFC records these existing vendor features so that future BGP work does not break them.

facts.label: Mechanisms
facts.value: Local AS, No Prepend Inbound, Replace Old AS, Internal BGP AS Migration

today: RFC 7705 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2015. The unit metadata shows it updates RFC 4271 and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why AS Numbers Get Migrated
sections.content:
RFC 7705 documents commonly used BGP mechanisms for Autonomous System Number (ASN) migration that are not formally part of BGP-4 (RFC 4271). They are local to one BGP speaker, need no negotiation with neighbors, and need not interwork with one another, so vendor implementations vary slightly. The RFC writes them down so new implementations succeed and future protocol work that reads, copies, manipulates or compares the AS_PATH attribute does not break them.

The need comes from mergers, acquisitions and divestitures. The goal is consistent configuration across the combined network, without lengthening the AS_PATH, because BGP path selection prefers the shortest AS_PATH and a longer one would likely cause sudden traffic shifts. By default a BGP session needs the ASN to match on both ends, so without these tools an ISP would have to coordinate a change with, in some cases, tens of thousands of customers.
sections.eli5: When two companies join, one of them has to change its name. These tricks let the change happen without calling every customer on the same day.

sections.title: The Migration Scenario
sections.content:
The RFC uses two ISPs, A with AS 64500 and B with AS 64510. AS 64500 is kept and AS 64510 is retired. Customer C (AS 64496) attaches to ISP B, and customer D (AS 64499) attaches to ISP A. Afterwards there is one network, ISP A', using AS 64500 everywhere, and external speakers must not see a longer AS_PATH. The examples use ASNs reserved for documentation, standing in for globally unique ASNs.

In a typical maintenance window, ISP B changes the global ASN of a Provider Edge (PE) router from 64510 to 64500. That breaks its eBGP sessions to customer devices still using 64510. So ISP B configures migration mechanisms on every customer-facing session: they let the router set up neighbors using the legacy ASN, and edit the AS_PATH on routes coming in and going out. The scenario assumes neither ISP uses BGP confederations.
sections.eli5: Two shops merge and keep one name. The staff at the old shop's counter change their badges, but still answer to the old name when regular customers call it.

sections.title: External Session Mechanisms
sections.content:
Three settings work on eBGP sessions toward customers.

  • Local AS puts a locally chosen ASN in the "My Autonomous System" field of the BGP OPEN message, instead of the global ASN, for a neighbor or group of neighbors. This is how the migrated PE keeps its session with customer C using 64510. By default it also prepends the old ASN to routes received from the customer.
  • No Prepend Inbound stops that prepend when the route is installed or sent to iBGP neighbors. Customer C's route stays at one ASN in length inside ISP A'. With both settings, CE-A sees AS_PATH 64500 64496. With Local AS alone it would see 64500 64510 64496.
  • Replace Old AS handles the outbound direction. In some implementations Local AS lengthens routes sent to the customer, so customer C would see 64510 64500 64499. With Replace Old AS the router appends only the Local AS value, and the customer sees 64510 64499, the same length as before migration.

These mechanisms MUST be configurable per neighbor or per neighbor group. A speaker SHOULD send OPEN with the local ASN, not the global one, so the neighbor does not raise a "Bad Peer AS" error.
sections.eli5: One trick lets the router answer to the old name. The second stops it writing the old name on mail it passes inward. The third stops it writing both names on mail it sends outward.

sections.title: Rules for Processing Updates
sections.content:
A speaker follows RFC 4271 Section 5.1.2 for updates from a Local AS neighbor, plus extra steps. Internally, it SHOULD append the Local AS ASN to the AS_PATH before installing the route or advertising to an iBGP neighbor. When advertising to an eBGP neighbor, it SHOULD first append the global ASN and then the Local AS value.

With No Prepend Inbound, the router MUST NOT append the Local AS ASN for installation or iBGP advertisement, but MUST still append the global ASN as normal when advertising to other local eBGP neighbors. With Replace Old AS, outbound updates MUST NOT include the global ASN and MUST append only the Local AS ASN.

An implementation MAY try to open the session with either the Local AS or the global ASN. If the session comes up on the global ASN, the AS_PATH changes SHOULD NOT be done. That lets the customer move to the new ASN without direct coordination. Four-octet ASNs vary slightly; the RFC points to RFC 6793.

If routers remain in the old ASN, they may accept routes with 64510 removed as if they had not passed through it, which can cause a loop that normal loop prevention does not catch. Careful filtering between old-ASN and new-ASN routers is needed.
sections.eli5: There are exact rules for which names get written on the envelope and when. If the customer has already switched to the new name, the mailroom leaves the envelope alone.

sections.title: Internal BGP AS Migration
sections.content:
Inside the network, the traditional method is to change the global ASN and every iBGP neighbor's remote ASN on each router at once. That is slow, resets sessions and risks visible outages, especially beyond a few dozen routers. The Internal BGP AS Migration mechanism lets an iBGP speaker form a single iBGP session using either the old or the new ASN, so both can coexist temporarily. It does not change the AS_PATH, and the session behaves like a normal iBGP session under RFC 4271 and RFC 4456.

The RFC's example uses redundant route reflectors (RRs), though they are not required.

  1. On one RR of a pair, change the global ASN to the retained one and enable the mechanism on all its iBGP sessions.
  2. Repeat on the other RR, removing the mechanism from sessions between RRs. It stays on RR client sessions.
  3. Establish iBGP sessions between all RRs of both networks, so the network looks like one.
  4. Migrate each legacy PE: change its global ASN and RR session ASN, and add the external mechanisms on its eBGP sessions in the same window.
  5. Remove the mechanism from the RRs in an orderly way.

This can take days or weeks, with the only observable disruption when each PE is changed.
sections.eli5: Inside the school, teachers answer to either the old or the new name for a while, so everyone can switch one at a time without the whole school stopping.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
The internal mechanism MUST be configurable per neighbor or neighbor group. When enabled, a speaker MUST accept an OPEN and establish an iBGP session if the ASN in "My Autonomous System" is either the global ASN or a locally configured ASN. It MUST send its own OPEN with one of the two. To avoid deadlock when both ends use the mechanism, it SHOULD send the global ASN first, and use the local ASN only if the peer answers with the "Bad Peer AS" error. It MUST treat updates as on a native iBGP session.

Appendix A says the mechanisms have multiple implementations in wide use and names Cisco, Juniper and Alcatel-Lucent, adding that the list is not exhaustive.
sections.eli5: If both sides use the trick, one tries the new name first and only switches to the old name if the other side says, "I do not know that name."

sections.title: Operations and Security
sections.content:
Legacy ASNs and the external mechanisms tend to stay a long time. ISPs often do not control customers' routers, and companies accumulate legacy ASNs through mergers, so the RFC advises planning for them to persist indefinitely. External legacy ASNs can last several years or longer. The internal mechanism is under one organization's control, so finishing it takes days to months, and it is good practice not to leave it enabled for a long time.

On security, the mechanisms are configured only on routers within one network, so access to router management interfaces should be restricted. The RFC also says BGP sessions SHOULD be protected with the TCP Authentication Option (RFC 5925) and the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (RFC 5082). It warns that AS_PATH manipulation, if it changes path length, could shift traffic and cause congestion.
sections.eli5: Old names tend to linger for years, so the mailroom plans to keep handling them. Only trusted staff should be allowed to change these rules.
